subject: mathematics
question_text: Prove that tan α = sin 2α/(1 + cos 2α), and use it to obtain the values of tan 15° and tan 22½°.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 8 TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS, Very Short Answer question 20, book p.86. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1 split rewards the proof first and the two substituted values second, because the question asks for a proof and then for two numbers, and a student who proves the identity but stops there has done half the work. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1 to Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory, under the 2026-27 pattern; Trigonometric Ratios and Transformations holds two of those ten slots. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Checked numerically: sin 2α/(1 + cos 2α) equals tan α to ten decimal places at α = 15°, 22½°, 37° and 110°, and it has no value at α = 90° where 1 + cos 2α = 0 — that is the cos α ≠ 0 condition, and it is stated on the page, not parked here. tan 15° = 0.2679491924 = 2 − √3 and tan 22½° = 0.4142135624 = √2 − 1.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity, and say which angles you would put in to get tan 15° and tan 22½°.

steps.margin_note: First mark. Choose the cos 2α form that leaves 2cos²α. The cancelling needs cos α ≠ 0, which is the same as 1 + cos 2α ≠ 0.
steps.memory_tip: Pick the cos 2α form that leaves 2cos²α: 1 + cos 2α = 2cos²α. Then one cos α cancels.

steps.why: The denominator 1 + cos 2α is exactly 2cos²α, so one cos α cancels from the top and the bottom and tan α is left. The cancelling needs cos α ≠ 0, which is the same condition as 1 + cos 2α ≠ 0.
common_mistakes: Cancelling cos α without stating that cos α is not 0.

steps.label: Put α = 15° and α = 22½°
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Choose α so that 2α is a standard angle. Both denominators come out as 2 + √3 and √2 + 1, and each rationalises to 1 because 4 − 3 = 1 and 2 − 1 = 1.
steps.memory_tip: Choose α so that 2α is a standard angle: 15° gives 30°, and 22½° gives 45°.

steps.why: Doubling the angle is what makes the identity useful: 2α is a standard angle (30° and 45°) even when α is not. Both answers come out already rationalised, because 4 − 3 = 1 and 2 − 1 = 1.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as 1/(2 + √3) without rationalising.
